title: File a punched card in a ring binder: snap the rings open, hang it on all three, press them shut
instruction: File the punched card in the binder: put it on all three rings and close the rings.
context: Filing a punched sheet in a ring binder is something nearly every student and office worker does, often daily. It is not pick-and-place. The rings are an over-centre toggle: two hinged steel plates under a sprung cover hold them either shut or open, so the two halves of a ring must be pinched and pulled apart firmly (about 12 N at the tips) until they snap open. Then the card's three 7.1 mm holes, 108 mm apart, must go over three 4 mm wires at once (about 1.5 mm of play per hole, 20 cm from the hand), and the card must be swung round the wire onto the page. Finally the halves must be squeezed until the rings snap shut, tips meeting, with nothing caught. Unlike loading a sheet protector (a pocket insertion, the binder only a prop), punching a card's holes, or closing a swing-top bottle's lever, the robot here works the ring mechanism itself and registers a sheet on three thin wires.
setup: Station table, one fixed layout (x forward from the arms, y to the left, heights above the table top; the arm bases are at x 0, y +-0.305 m). Binder: a standard US 1 in round-ring Letter binder (for example the Avery Economy 1" round-ring binder): two 292 x 257 mm covers of 3 mm vinyl-covered board and a 36 mm spine, opened flat (550 mm across) with its spine along x, centred on x 0.27 m, taped to the table with two strips of masking tape across its covers. The front cover is on the left (y 0.031 to 0.288 m), the spine at y -0.005 to 0.031 m, the back cover on the right (y -0.262 to -0.005 m). The ring mechanism is riveted to the back cover with its centre line at y -0.03 m: a nickel-plated steel cover 250 x 32 mm (x 0.145 to 0.395 m), 13 mm above the table, over two hinged steel plates; three round rings of 4 mm wire, 25.4 mm inside diameter, 108 mm apart at x 0.162, 0.270 and 0.378 m, their tops 37 mm above the table. The rings start shut. Card: a Letter (279 x 216 mm) sheet of 110 lb white index card stock (199 g/m2, 12 g), three-hole punched along one long edge (7.1 mm holes, 108 mm apart, centres 9.5 mm from the edge), with two printed lines. It waits in the front slot of a Letter-size wire step file (a desktop incline sorter, for example the Fellowes Wire Step File 72614, about 308 x 257 mm and 300 mm tall: steel mesh, three slots stepping up away from the binder, a 10 mm front lip, dividers 160 and 230 mm tall and a 300 mm back), standing on the table on the right of the binder with its slots along x, centred on x 0.27 m, its front edge at y -0.270 m. The card stands in the front slot on its punched edge (that edge against the lip at y -0.276 m), centred on x 0.27 m, leaning back 15 degrees on the first divider's top edge; its top edge is 212 mm above the table, 50 mm above the divider. Both arms start in their ready pose.
scoring: Scored every control step from the card's and the ring plates' poses; the score at the end of the trial counts. A ring is on the card when its wire passes through one of the card's holes; a ring is shut when its two tips are within 1 mm of each other, and open when they are 10 mm or more apart. 1.0: the card is on all three rings, all three rings are shut, no part of either gripper is within 2 cm of the card or of any ring, and the card and ring tips are still (neither moved more than 1 mm over the preceding 1 s), all held together for 1 s (20 control steps in a row). 0.75: at some point the card was on all three rings with all three rings shut. 0.5: at some point the card was on all three rings. 0.25: at some point all three rings were open. Otherwise 0. A card on only one or two rings, hooked on the tips without a ring through a hole, or lying across shut rings earns nothing beyond the open rings; a ring pulled part-way and let go springs shut and earns nothing. In a real trial: a photo shows each ring's wire through a hole; the tip gap is checked with a ruler (shut: the tips touch with no visible gap); the 10 mm opening is read from the video against a ruler; the 2 cm clearance is checked on the video against the same ruler.
reset_notes: Squeeze any ring to shut the rings with no card on them, then stand the card back in the step file's front slot, punched edge down against the lip, centred on x 0.27 m, leaning back on the divider. Nothing is consumed.
fidelity: Rigid bodies at real size and mass. The rings ride on two hinged 13 mm steel plates whose outer edges a preloaded spring (the cover) pushes together: a real over-centre toggle, joint limits as the stops (22 mm open). Pulling the tips apart takes 12 N, an estimate (no published figure). Card: rigid 0.5 mm plate (real card stock flexes); holes are real collision gaps. Pad-on-wire friction 1.0 (dry rubber on steel).
scores: Dream-1 run: 0.0 (arms stayed near their ready pose; rings never opened, card left in the step file); demo: 1.0 (full score at step 855, episode ended with success at step 874)
